passage: The rain had been falling for two hours, and the class was stuck in the corridor waiting for the buses. The seating chart was taped to the wall, sorted by last month's ranks. Front row: the toppers. Back row: the backbenchers. Lalremsiami, at the top of the list, pressed her folder to her chest. Her latest mark was 88, not 95, and she had not told a soul. At the back, Siddharth sat on the floor with his pen still in the bag. “Why bother?” he said to nobody. “I'm the last-row type.” Two boys laughed and agreed. Lalremsiami glanced at Siddharth, then at her mark, and pulled her folder in tighter.

qa.q: Where did the seating chart on the corridor wall place the toppers?
qa.a: The toppers were in the front row of the chart.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami press her folder to her chest?
qa.a: Lalremsiami seems afraid that anyone might find out her mark was 88 and not 95; as a topper she fears any failure.

qa.q: What might help Siddharth start trying again?
qa.a: Siddharth might be helped by someone who treats him as more than a last-row type, such as a teacher who notices one improvement, or classmates who study with him.

qa.q: How might Siddharth see Lalremsiami's place at the top of the list?
qa.a: Siddharth may see the topper's life as easy, not knowing that Lalremsiami hides the 88 and pulls her folder tight; the label works both ways.

grounding: Students grouped as toppers and backbenchers begin to live up to the label: one called weak stops trying while one called clever fears any failure.

passage: In the coaching centre, students of Batch A sat at the front near the fan, and Batch C sat by the door. Hafsa was in Batch C, and everybody knew it. Last week she got the top mark on the chemistry chapter, but the teacher read the marks out by batch and hers sounded like an accident. Zainab, from Batch A, turned to her at the water cooler. “You got the highest? I got fourteen wrong on mine, please don't tell.” Hafsa shrugged, folded her paper small and said, “Don't worry, it was an easy chapter.” Back in her seat, she left the next worksheet unopened and watched the door.

qa.q: Where did Batch C sit in the coaching centre?
qa.a: Batch C sat by the door.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa say “it was an easy chapter” after getting the highest mark?
qa.a: Hafsa seems to have accepted the label of Batch C and expects her mark to look like an accident, so she plays it down and folds her paper small.

qa.q: What could the teacher change so that Hafsa keeps trying?
qa.a: The teacher could stop reading marks out by batch, notice Hafsa's top mark as real effort and look at each student's own progress.

qa.q: What might Zainab be afraid of when she says, “please don't tell”?
qa.a: Zainab may fear that a Batch A student with fourteen wrong looks like a failure, showing that a clever label brings its own fear of falling short.

grounding: A student labelled weak stops trying while a student labelled clever fears any failure, in a coaching centre grouped by batch.

passage:
Dear Vishal bhaiya,
You asked why I sounded strange on the phone. Here's the truth. In our school, the first row is called 'the toppers' and the last row 'the backbenchers'. I've been in the first row since Class 6. Last week I got 71 in the chemistry test, my lowest ever, and Sir read the marks aloud. Someone at the back said, 'Topper down!' and everyone laughed. Since then I can't sleep properly before tests. I'm scared that if I slip once more, I'll lose the one thing people know me for.
The odd part is that Deepa at the back, whom everyone calls weak, understood the practical better than me. She's stopped raising her hand, though, because 'backbenchers don't know anything'.
Can you call on Sunday?
Nandini

qa.q: What mark did Nandini get in the chemistry test?
qa.a: 71, the lowest ever.

qa.q: What is Nandini afraid of now?
qa.a: Nandini feels scared and pressured that one more slip will cost the 'topper' identity people know Nandini for.

qa.q: What could the teacher change to weaken these labels?
qa.a: Stop reading marks aloud, mix the seating, and praise work like Deepa's practical so no one is fixed as topper or weak.

qa.q: How does the 'backbencher' label seem to affect Deepa?
qa.a: Although she understood the practical well, she has stopped raising her hand, believing backbenchers don't know anything.

grounding: A student labelled a topper fears any failure, while a classmate labelled weak stops trying.

passage: Funny you ask about labels, Hafsa. This is Hemant, proud ex-backbencher, speaking. In Class 9 our teacher made a seating chart by marks. I landed in the last row with five others, and after that the teachers just stopped asking us anything. So we stopped trying. Why study if everyone had already decided? I used to draw cars in my notebook during maths. Then in Class 11 a new maths teacher mixed the rows every week and one day gave me a problem about car speeds. I solved it on the board. The class went quiet. I remember thinking, wait, I'm not weak, I was just parked. It took me a whole year to really believe that, but it started there.

qa.q: How did the Class 9 teacher decide the seating?
qa.a: By marks, with a seating chart.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when solving the car-speed problem on the board?
qa.a: Hemant felt surprised and quietly proud, thinking 'I'm not weak, I was just parked.'

qa.q: Which choice of the Class 11 teacher helped, and why?
qa.a: Mixing the rows every week and giving Hemant a problem about car speeds, which broke the label and offered a real chance to succeed.

qa.q: How might the other five in the last row have felt in Class 9?
qa.a: They were likely discouraged and ignored too, since the teachers stopped asking them anything.

grounding: A student placed in the 'weak' back row stops trying until a teacher breaks the label.

passage: Monday, first week of Class 9: Urmila ma'am split the class into 'A group' and 'support group' by last year's marks. Darshan saw his name on the support list and felt his face burn. His friend Mehul was in A group. Two weeks later, Thursday: Darshan had stopped doing homework. 'Support group doesn't get the hard questions anyway,' he told Mehul. Mehul, for his part, had cried in the washroom after getting a B, terrified of dropping out of A group. A month later, Friday: after the parents' meeting, Urmila ma'am mixed the groups and gave everyone the same worksheet. Darshan finished the first three sums and hesitated over the fourth. He didn't hand it in blank.

qa.q: How did Urmila ma'am split the class in the first week?
qa.a: Into 'A group' and 'support group' by last year's marks.

qa.q: Why had Darshan stopped doing homework by the second week?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and ashamed of the 'support' label, believing the hard questions weren't meant for him anyway.

qa.q: What change did Urmila ma'am make, and why might it help?
qa.a: She mixed the groups and gave everyone the same worksheet, removing the label so Darshan could try again.

qa.q: How did the label affect Mehul, who was in A group?
qa.a: He was terrified of dropping out of A group and cried after getting a B, so the 'clever' label brought him fear too.

grounding: Over a month, ability labels make one student stop trying and another fear failure, until the groups are mixed.

passage: You're worried about the new sections, Nilesh? Let your Anand Chacha tell you something. In Class 9 our school split us: A section for the "toppers", D for the rest. I landed in D. The first week, the maths teacher said, "D section, just pass, that's enough." And you know, I stopped trying. Why lift the pen if the teacher has already decided? My friend Mukund went to A. You'd think he was lucky. He used to shake before every test, because one bad mark and he would be "fallen". He once hid a sixty-two from his father for a month. Neither of us was what the board said. It took a Class 11 teacher asking me to explain a sum to the whole class before I believed I could think.

qa.q: Which section was Anand placed in during Class 9?
qa.a: Anand landed in D section.

qa.q: Why did young Anand stop trying after the first week?
qa.a: He felt written off and discouraged when the teacher said D section only needed to pass, so effort seemed pointless.

qa.q: What turning point helped Anand, and why did it work?
qa.a: A Class 11 teacher asked him to explain a sum to the whole class, which treated him as someone who could think instead of a label.

qa.q: What was it like for Mukund to be in the topper section?
qa.a: Mukund lived in fear: one bad mark could make him "fallen", so he shook before tests and hid a sixty-two from his father.

grounding: Anand Chacha recalls how labels of toppers and the rest made one student stop trying and another fear any failure.
